title: Sound and image, in and out of sync
introduction: This week's art class was about the relationship between sound and image, and specifically how they synchronise — or deliberately do not. We looked at the different ways sound and picture can be pulled together or held apart, and finished with the idea of a sound perspective, where sound design puts you inside a character's head rather than simply showing you what they see.
related_work: We began with the McGurk effect, where a mouth that moves one way and a sound that says another makes you hear the sound that matches the mouth: vision overrules hearing, and that tells you something about which sense leads. From there the key idea was that synchronisation is not a switch but a spectrum, running from perfectly in sync to completely apart, and that film often sits in a 'pseudo-sync' zone in between, using the tension to make you think. Films also rely on an audio-visual contract: the sound and picture are made separately and stitched together, yet we accept them as one world. That is why enhancement works — a boxing punch does not sound like its screen effect in real life, but synced to the image it feels true. We then looked at the different jobs sound can do. A train whistle can bridge two scenes and link them in time and space. In Apocalypse Now, the mismatch between a ceiling fan and helicopter blades pulls the image into an unreal space and into the character's mind. In Tom and Jerry, music locks exactly onto footsteps and breathing to exaggerate every emotion. Finally, the class turned to perspective: just as a close-up or tracking shot puts us in a character's eyes, sound can put us in their ears, and A Silent Voice uses this so we seem to hear a character's inner monologue.
method: I went through the examples slowly and asked the same question of each one: what does this kind of sync, or this kind of mismatch, do to the person watching? That turned out to be the most useful way to organise the material, because each technique is really an instruction to the viewer about where to put their attention.
results_discussion: What stayed with me is that sound is doing much more than decorating the picture. The McGurk effect shows how easily vision takes charge, and the sync spectrum shows that the interesting work happens in the middle, in the gap between sound and image, where uncertainty lives. The audio-visual contract explains why we rarely question that gap: we want the world to cohere, so we help it along. Enhancement is where this gets creative — a punch sound that is not physically real still reads as real, because the sync invites us to accept it. The examples then split into clear functions: sound can bridge scenes, stretch space, or lock onto action to exaggerate emotion. But the idea that hit me hardest was sound perspective, because it turns sound from something outside the story into a way of being inside a character. In A Silent Voice, hearing the world as the character hears it is what lets you feel their interior. That feels directly useful for my own work, where I have been thinking about how to guide someone's attention through gesture and interaction — now I see sound as a second channel for doing exactly that.
conclusion_future_work: My takeaway is that synchronisation is a creative material, not a technical requirement. Sound can confirm the image, contradict it, or pull the viewer into someone's head, and the choice between those is a design decision. For my own work I want to think about sound and image together from the start, not add sound at the end. The question I am carrying forward is simple: what do I want the sound to make someone feel or believe, the way these films made me believe in spaces and thoughts that were not really there.
